sources.title: Spatial and Sociosexual Behavior During Pair Formation in Common Marmosets (Callithrix jacchus)
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods—Subjects and Housing, Experimental Design, Spatial Proximity, Sociosexual Behavior; Results; study limitations.
sources.scope: Captive adult common marmosets at the UZH Primate Station, Switzerland: three adult males and three adult females in eight analyzed mixed-sex dyads; partners were assigned by researchers and repeated short visual exposures were tested from February through August 2022.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated in the publisher's Rights and permissions section.
sources.rightsEvidenceLocator: Publisher Rights and permissions section; separately credited third-party material may have different terms.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Paraphrased article text only; no figures, tables, images, or supplementary-file content is copied.
sources.attribution: Wienand L, Burkart JM, Wierucka K. (2026). Spatial and Sociosexual Behavior During Pair Formation in Common Marmosets (Callithrix jacchus). International Journal of Primatology 47:698–719. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-026-00553-2. CC BY 4.0. Claims are paraphrased.

claims.text: Before assigned pair formation, repeated short visual exposures of initially unfamiliar captive common marmosets were associated with a model-estimated 32.3% decrease in direct interindividual distance per exposure. After pair formation, mate status had no clear association with direct distance (P=0.37).
claims.scope: Eight mixed-sex dyads of six captive adults at one Swiss station; this short assay does not describe wild grouping or mate choice.

claims.text: Across 91 analyzed recordings, the study recorded 436 sociosexual behaviors. A pooled model estimated about 1.2 more scan-counts across nine scans in a session before pair formation than after it (P=0.023); after pairing, observed counts were lower in pair-mate than less familiar extra-pair dyads.
claims.scope: Exploratory captive observations from researcher-assigned pairs, not estimates of wild mating behavior, sexual exclusivity, or population-wide social organization.

gaps: The added pair-formation evidence is one exploratory captive assay from six adults at a single station; partner assignment did not allow mate choice.
Natural dispersal, wild social relationships, long-term pair maintenance, and population variation remain unassessed.
